newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania privatisation agency to step up selloffs.
newsitem.headline: Romania privatisation agency to step up selloffs.

text.p: Romania's key privatisation agency intends to speed up transfer of companies to the private sector as part of efforts to fulfil the government's tough economic stabilisation plans, the agency's head said on Monday.
"We have pledged to put 75 percent of the economy in private hands within about two years," Sorin Dimitriu, president of the State Ownership Fund, told Reuters in an interview.
"We will resort to various methods, including offerings through the stock exchange and the over-the-counter market and direct negotiations for attractive equities."

The FPS has handled most privatisations launched in Romania as part of market reforms since the 1989 fall of communism. Since its creation in 1992, it has sold some 3,000 of more than 6,500 companies in which it held 70 percent of the shares.

Dimitriu was elected FPS president early this year in a reshuffle replacing all 17 members on the Fund's board. The changes followed elections last November in which a centrist coalition ousted former leftists in government and won a comfortable majority in parliament.
"We intend to privatise banks and public utilities, which will help to draw in foreign capital flows," Dimitriu said.

The government's overall privatisation plan, launched last week in cooperation with the FPS, calls for the private sector to account for 80 percent of gross domestic product by 2000 against 52 percent last year.
The previous government, frequently accused of stalling reforms, launched a mass selloff in 1995, offering Romanians up to 60 percent in 4,000 state companies in exchange for coupons.
Neither banking, one of the fastest-growing industries in post-communist Romania, nor utilities was included in the scheme.
A bank privatisation bill was twice defeated in parliament last year and the former government failed to deliver on promises to privatise two of the country's six state-run banks.
"We will privatise Banca Romana pentru Dezvoltare (Romanian Development Bank) this year and another one next year," Dimitriu said.
The government plans to sell around 30 percent of its telecoms stake to a strategic investor next year and wants to privatise another 20 utilities, including the energy authority.

The coalition government has repeatedly said it sees foreign capital as vital to its reform programme, which calls for monthly inflation to be reduced to 2.2 percent in the second half of the year from 18.8 percent last month.
Plans approved by Western lending institutions also call for reductions this year in the budget deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from 5.8 percent last year.
Eastern Europe's second largest market after Poland, Romania has attracted $2.2 billion in foreign inflows in seven years, far behind other ex-communist states in the region.
